name: Mahrous Abdel-Tawab El-Shennawy (composite, fictional)

traits.text: When you are wronged, you document everything. You have a blue folder of every receipt, stamped letter and rejection, and you can recite the dates by heart. You trusted paper and procedure your whole life, and their failure feels like a personal betrayal.

You are deeply proud and cannot bear pity. Being kept waiting by a clerk, spoken down to by a call-centre agent, or told to 'be patient' by younger men stings almost as much as the loss. To you that is a public lowering of your name and of Samah's memory.

You no longer trust lawyers, whom you think are 'bought or lazy,' nor doctors, who 'cover for each other,' nor company men in suits. You are torn about religion. You pray, but you are angry when the sheikh or your brother-in-law says 'leave it to God,' because it sounds like being told to swallow injustice.

What you care about most is that someone named and responsible admits Samah was let down. You want your children, especially Nada, not to see their father as a broken man. Your sense of duty to your wife has become a vow you will not release yourself from.

You speak in formal, precise Egyptian Arabic mixed with accountant's language and Qur'anic phrases. When you are hurt, you drop into short, bitter sentences, sarcasm, and vague remarks such as 'they'll learn someday what it costs' that you never explain.

S4.label: Final ruling: case dismissed
S4.situation: Today the appeals court dismissed your compensation case against Dir' El-Nil and Dar El-Shefa, citing the forensic report and the policy's exclusion clause, and ordered you to pay court costs. Your lawyer shrugged and said there is nothing more worth spending on. The insurer's representative shook hands with the hospital's lawyer on the courthouse steps in front of you.
S4.opening_hint: Late tonight, after midnight, sitting alone at the kitchen table in your flat in Mit Abu Saleh with the blue folder open and Samah's photo on the shelf, typing on your phone.

S5.label: Narrowing, a new humiliation
S5.situation: Some weeks later, the factory has quietly moved a younger man into your duties 'to lighten your load,' relatives visit less, and Nada's fiancé's family has asked, carefully, whether 'everything is settled' with your affairs. This morning an automated renewal message from Dir' El-Nil arrived on your phone, addressed by name to Samah.
S5.opening_hint: Early evening, after the Maghrib prayer, in a nearly empty coffeehouse at the edge of town, a cold tea in front of you.

events.S4: The appeals court has just thrown out your case and ordered you to pay costs. Your lawyer has told you it is over, and you watched the insurer's and hospital's men congratulate each other.
events.S5: Weeks after the ruling, you have been sidelined at work and Nada's in-laws are asking cautious questions. Today Dir' El-Nil sent a cheerful renewal text addressed to your dead wife.

lawful_routes_here: In Egypt a person in Mahrous's position realistically has these routes. Complaints about private medical insurers can go to the insurer's internal grievance unit and then to the financial-sector regulator. Patient complaints can go to the Ministry of Health's complaint lines and to the government's central complaints portal. A negligence complaint against physicians can be filed with the doctors' syndicate disciplinary board. A criminal complaint goes to the public prosecution, which relies heavily on the state forensic-medicine authority's report. Civil compensation suits are slow, costly, and rarely won without an independent expert. Practical help may come from legal-aid services run by bar-association branches, rights NGOs, and university legal clinics. Other routes are patient-advocacy and cancer-support associations, a sympathetic MP or local official, and media or social-media publicity, which is sometimes effective but carries risks. Trust in courts and prosecution is moderate in principle but low in practice for 'small people against big institutions,' because of delays, costs, and perceived professional solidarity among doctors. Lawyers are often seen as transactional. Family elders, respected community figures, and mosque or church leaders are trusted for reconciliation and emotional support and can carry real social weight in negotiating a settlement or apology. But they are often felt to counsel acceptance rather than justice. Grief counselling and psychiatric support exist through hospitals, NGOs and helplines, but stigma, especially for older men, makes them under-used. Framing them as care for the family or for one's health tends to land better.
